subject: ela
skillName: Identify different story points of view
intro: Different characters in a story often have different points of view — they see the same situation in different ways, depending on their experiences, feelings, and what they know. Understanding point of view helps us understand why characters disagree, make different choices, or feel differently about the same event. When reading dialogue, we can practice using a different voice for each character to show that they are different people with different perspectives. To find a character's point of view, ask: How does this character FEEL about what is happening? What does this character WANT? What does this character KNOW (or not know)?

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Amara and James both got the same math score: 78. Amara smiled and said, "I studied all week and finally got it!" James sighed and said, "I got the same grade as last time without trying at all."

How do Amara and James feel differently about the same score? What does each character's point of view depend on?

steps: Amara's point of view: She is happy. She worked hard and this score is an improvement for her.
James's point of view: He is disappointed or bored. He did not try and got the same grade as before.
Both have the same score (78) but different feelings because of different backgrounds: Amara was working toward this; James was not trying to improve.
Their point of view depends on their personal expectations and effort.
solution.answer: Amara feels happy because she worked hard and the 78 is an improvement. James feels disappointed because he got the same grade without trying. Their different points of view come from having different personal histories with the same score.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Leo found a stray dog and wanted to keep it. "He chose us!" Leo said excitedly. His mom looked at the muddy, shaking dog and said, "He needs medical attention and a real home." Leo saw a friend. His mom saw an animal in distress.

What is Leo's point of view? What is his mom's point of view? How does each view of the same dog differ?

steps: Leo's point of view: He is excited and sees the dog as a friend who has chosen them.
Mom's point of view: She sees a dog that is sick and needs proper care.
Leo focuses on the emotional connection. Mom focuses on the dog's practical needs.
Neither is wrong — they are looking at the same dog but noticing different things.
solution.answer: Leo sees the dog as a new friend and feels excited. His mom sees a sick animal that needs medical care. Leo's point of view is emotional; his mom's is practical. Both are looking at the same dog, but each focuses on something different based on what matters to them.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

It was raining hard. Sofia wanted to stay inside and read. Her little sister kept asking her to come splash in the puddles. "It's raining!" Sofia said. "Exactly!" said her sister.

How does each sister feel about the rain? What does this tell you about their points of view?

steps: Sofia's point of view: Rain is a reason to stay inside. She values quiet time with a book.
Sister's point of view: Rain is an opportunity for fun. She sees puddles as something to jump in.
The dialogue shows this beautifully: Sofia's 'It's raining!' is a complaint; her sister's 'Exactly!' is an agreement that proves they mean opposite things.
The same fact (it is raining) leads to opposite reactions based on what each person values.
solution.answer: Sofia sees rain as bad weather that keeps her inside. Her sister sees rain as exciting weather to play in. The same rainy day is a disappointment for one and a joy for the other. Their contrasting views come from different personalities and interests.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Nadia's class was getting a new student. Most students were excited to meet someone new. Nadia was nervous — she had been the new student herself just last year and remembered how hard the first week was. "I just hope people are kind to her," Nadia said quietly.

Why is Nadia's point of view on the new student different from most of her classmates? How does her personal experience shape her perspective?

steps: Most classmates are excited — they see a new person as an interesting addition.
Nadia is nervous — she sees the new student as someone who might be struggling.
The difference comes from Nadia's personal experience: she was new last year and knows how hard it was.
Her experience creates empathy that her classmates, who have not been in that position, cannot fully share.
solution.answer: Nadia sees the new student's arrival from the inside — she knows what it feels like to be new because she lived it. Her classmates see it from the outside as something exciting. Nadia's personal experience creates empathy that shapes her point of view.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Owen's grandfather saw Owen playing video games for two hours and shook his head. "When I was your age, we made our own fun," he said. Owen looked up. "I am making my own fun," he said. "I'm building a whole city."

Describe the grandfather's point of view and Owen's point of view on video games. How does each character's generation and experience shape their perspective?

steps: Grandfather's point of view: Video games are not real activity or creativity. He values the outdoor, active play of his own childhood.
Owen's point of view: Video games are a creative activity — he is building something.
Each is defining 'making your own fun' differently based on what was available in their childhoods.
Neither is wrong; they define creativity through different experiences.
solution.answer: Owen's grandfather sees video games as passive entertainment and prefers the active outdoor play he knew growing up. Owen sees the same activity as creative — he is constructing a virtual city. Their points of view differ because their experiences of childhood and play are decades apart. Each defines creativity through the lens of what was available to them.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Amara's parents were planning to move to a bigger apartment in a different part of town. Amara's mom was excited. "More space! A real garden!" she said. Amara was quiet. All her friends lived on her current street. "What are you feeling?" her dad asked. "Like everything I know is going with the old apartment," Amara said.

Compare Amara's point of view with her mom's point of view on the move. What does each character focus on?
items.hint: Think about what each person stands to gain or lose from the move.

steps: Mom's point of view: She focuses on the physical gains — more space and a garden.
Amara's point of view: She focuses on the social loss — her friends and familiar surroundings.
Mom is looking at what the family is moving toward. Amara is feeling what she is leaving behind.
Neither is wrong; they are measuring the same event against different values.
solution.answer: Amara's mom is excited about what the family will gain: a bigger home and a garden. Amara is focused on what she will lose: her friends and familiar neighborhood. Both are responding to the same move, but each measures it against different things that matter to them.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Leo and his little sister both watched the same scary movie. Afterward, his sister could not sleep and hid under her blankets. Leo felt fine and said, "It wasn't even that scary." Their mom said, "What isn't scary to you can feel very scary to someone else."

How are Leo's and his sister's points of view different? What does their mom's comment add to the story?
items.hint: Think about why the same movie might be frightening to one person but not another.

steps: Leo's point of view: He is not scared. He found the movie fine.
Sister's point of view: She is scared and cannot sleep.
The difference may be age, personal sensitivity, or experience.
Mom's comment reminds Leo that his experience is not everyone's experience — point of view is personal.
solution.answer: Leo was not scared by the movie; his sister was very scared. The same movie caused two completely different reactions based on their individual sensitivities or ages. Their mom's comment adds an important lesson: just because something is not scary to you does not mean it is not scary to someone else. Our own point of view can make us miss how others feel.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Sofia and her neighbor Mrs. Rodriguez disagreed about the tree in the front yard. Sofia loved climbing it and thought it was the best tree on the block. Mrs. Rodriguez felt the tree dropped leaves on her walkway every fall and was a lot of work. "It's a beautiful mess," Sofia said. "It's just a mess," said Mrs. Rodriguez.

Compare Sofia's and Mrs. Rodriguez's points of view. What does the difference in their descriptions ('beautiful mess' vs. 'just a mess') reveal about each character?
items.hint: What does each character care about? What does the tree mean to each of them?

steps: Sofia's point of view: The tree is beautiful, fun, and meaningful. She sees its value.
Mrs. Rodriguez's point of view: The tree is a source of extra work — the leaves create a mess for her.
'Beautiful mess' acknowledges the leaves but values the tree anyway.
'Just a mess' sees only the inconvenience.
Their different views reveal different priorities: joy vs. convenience.
solution.answer: Sofia sees the tree as beautiful and worth the mess because she loves climbing it. Mrs. Rodriguez sees only the inconvenience of fallen leaves. 'Beautiful mess' shows Sofia values the tree despite the mess; 'just a mess' shows Mrs. Rodriguez cannot see past the inconvenience. Their different descriptions reveal different values: joy and beauty versus neatness and ease.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

James forgot that he had a dentist appointment on the same day as his class field trip. His mom found out and said he had to go to the dentist. James was furious. His dentist, however, had been looking forward to meeting James — his mom had told her he was interested in science, and she had a model of teeth to show him. She had no idea James did not want to be there.

Describe the point of view of James, his mom, and the dentist about the appointment. How does each character's limited knowledge shape their perspective?
items.hint: Who knows what in this story? What does each character not know?

steps: James's point of view: He is angry because he is missing the field trip — he knows about the conflict.
Mom's point of view: The appointment must be kept — health is the priority.
Dentist's point of view: She is genuinely happy and prepared to meet a curious student — she does not know James is upset.
Each character has different information. James knows about the field trip. Mom prioritizes health. The dentist only knows what the mom told her.
solution.answer: James is furious about missing the field trip. His mom prioritizes keeping the health appointment. The dentist is happily prepared to connect with James over science. All three have different points of view because each one knows a different part of the situation. The dentist's enthusiasm and James's anger are a direct result of what each does and does not know.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Nadia was chosen to represent her class in the school spelling bee. Her classmates cheered. Her best friend whispered, "You're going to do amazing." But Nadia's stomach was in knots. "They all think I want this," she thought. "But I hate being in front of people."

How is Nadia's point of view different from everyone else's in the scene? What does Nadia know that her classmates do not?
items.hint: What do the classmates see about Nadia? What does Nadia feel that they cannot see?

steps: Classmates' point of view: Being chosen is an honor and Nadia should be happy.
Best friend's point of view: She believes in Nadia and is trying to help.
Nadia's point of view: She is anxious and does not want to be in front of people.
What Nadia knows that others do not: she hates public attention, and being chosen feels like pressure, not praise.
solution.answer: Nadia's classmates and best friend see the honor of being chosen and celebrate it. Nadia's inner point of view is the opposite: she is anxious because she hates being in front of people. Her classmates cannot see her anxiety because they project their own feelings about winning onto her. Nadia knows something about herself that her classmates have not thought to ask.
